patch.objective: Explain the cardiovascular response to exercise: higher heart rate and stroke volume, and blood redirected to working muscle
secondaryObjectives: Calculate cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume, and explain how preload, contractility and afterload change stroke volume

sources.cite: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.4 Cardiac Physiology and 20.4 Homeostatic Regulation of the Vascular System
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through summarizing fetches of both pages. 19.4: CO = SV x HR; in exercise 'HR may increase to 150 bpm' and 'SV can also increase from 70 to approximately 130 mL', so CO rises to about 19.5 L/min, '4-5 times the resting rate'. 20.4: exercise brings 'selective vasodilation in the skeletal muscles, heart, lungs, liver, and integument' (Table 20.3: skeletal muscle flow 1,200 mL/min at rest to 12,500 at maximal exercise). The PTPREREQ course cites this book. Why the case's stopping rule makes sense: with cardiac output rising, systolic pressure should rise as the workload rises; a fall with rising grade means the heart is not keeping up.

sources.note: Relayed from the PTA case pta-back-pain-new-bladder-symptoms, which read it 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes, not re-read: only the physical therapist performs evaluation, reexamination and modification of the plan of care; the PTA collects selected data and modifies an intervention 'to ensure patient or client safety and comfort'; a PT supervisory visit is made on the PTA's request for a reexamination and 'in response to a change in the patient's or client's medical status'.

sources.cite: APTA Acute Care and APTA Cardiovascular and Pulmonary, Adult Vital Sign Interpretation in Acute Care Guide 2021 (boards approved March and April 2021)
sources.note: Relayed from the DPT case icu-early-mobility, which read it 2026-11-11 through a text extraction of the PDF, not re-read: normal exercise response, HR up about 10 beats/min and SBP up about 10 mmHg per MET; stop criteria include an SBP drop over 10 mmHg with increasing workload, new or worsening dysrhythmia, RR over 40, unable to speak comfortably, SpO2 under 90% or a drop of 4% or more.
Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.
